newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel stands firm against PLO on "terrorism".
newsitem.headline: Israel stands firm against PLO on "terrorism".

text.p: Crown Prince Hassan of Jordan failed in talks with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Wednesday to persuade Israel to end sanctions it imposed on Palestinians after a double suicide bombing.

"If they begin to fight terrorism, we will review the various steps that were taken in order to make them fight terrorism," Netanyahu said after a three-hour meeting with King Hussein's younger brother.
"We are firm in the measures we have taken," the right-wing Israeli leader said.

Israel sealed off the West Bank and Gaza Strip after last Wednesday's twin bombing killed 15 people including the two bombers in a Jerusalem street market. Palestinian President Yasser Arafat condemned the closure as collective punishment.

A Jordanian official, who asked not to be identified, said the main purpose of the crown prince's talks in Jerusalem was to "restart Palestinian-Israeli negotiations and end Israel's punitive measures against the Palestinians".
In Syria, official newspapers warned that Netanyahu was pushing the Middle East towards a "grave explosion" and urged Arabs to prepare for "military and political" battles with Israel.
The newspapers said peace was impossible as long as Israel proceeded with building Jewish settlements on land occupied from Arabs in the 1967 Middle East war.

Even before Wednesday's meeting, Israeli officials publicly put Jordan on notice that the Jewish state's demands on Arafat to crack down on Moslem militants it believes were behind the attack would dominate the discussions.
Israeli commentators said the prospect of coming away empty-handed led to King Hussein's decision not to travel to Jerusalem and send his brother in his place.
Netanyahu's office had originally announced the monarch would visit. Instead, the prime minister will see King Hussein in Jordan next week.
Crown Prince Hassan described the situation as "a very dangerous crisis".

"There can be no peace without security and there can be no security without peace," he said. "We must not forget the basic issues...Jerusalem, refugees, water, borders," Prince Hassan told the news conference.
"But unless we overcome positively the daily issues and stand together responsibly on the issues of security it will be hard to move on to a comprehensive solution."

After the Jerusalem attack, the deadliest against Israelis in a year, Netanyahu suspended a resumption of Israel-PLO talks at committee level on so-called confidence-building measures such as opening air and sea ports in Gaza.
Chief PLO negotiator Saeb Erekat accused Israel on Wednesday of treating Palestinians like hostages.

"The Israeli measures indicated the Israeli government's readiness to launch a war on the Palestinian Authority, President Arafat and the Palestinian people," Erekat told a news conference in the West Bank.

He said Arafat had given King Hussein and Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak a list of "12 oppressive measures practiced by the Israeli government against our people" and asked the two leaders to play "a distinct role to end the current crisis".
The edicts included, Erekat said, the suspension of talks with the PLO, a "siege of Palestinian cities, villages and refugee camps" and stopping the transfer of money to the PA.
Israeli President Ezer Weizman, after a separate meeting with Crown Prince Hassan, appeared to take a softer line than Netanyahu.

"I hope that very soon the military authority will find a way to lessen the tightness on the West Bank and...we fully realise that it is not an easy life when you can't go from one place to another," said Weizman, whose post is largely ceremonial.
Netanyahu said it was not Israel's intention to inflict "undue suffering" on Palestinians and it had allowed humanitarian supplies of food and medicine into self-ruled areas.
But in answer to a question he rejected a U.S. call to unfreeze 70 million shekels ($19.8 million) of tax revenues which Israel has withheld from the Palestinian Authority since the bombing.

Netanyahu preceded his talks with the crown prince, who was accompanied by Prime Minister Abdul-Salam al-Majali, by visiting the scene of last week's carnage, the Mahane Yehuda market where he donned a skullcap and lit a memorial candle.

"Bibi, Bibi," the crowd chanted, using Netanyahu's nickname in a sign of support for the Likud party leader who won election last year by pledging to boost security in the wake of a series of suicide bombings that killed 57 people.
